I know it's best to try the smallest value of K that makes biologically sense as a maximum and results in model convergence. I am just curious if anyone know why time increases exponentially rather than linearly? Is it just that convergence on the maximum likelihood gets less stable when including the area under the far tail end of the curve? I haven't spent much time coding my own ML functions, so I'm not really familiar with the these issues, just curious.

Thanks,
Dan

messages.subject_clean: using pcountOpen to detect changes in apparent survival
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to run some simulations to estimate the power to detect changes in stream amphibian abundance due to dam construction using a BACI design, and I am a little stuck with parameterizing the pcountOpen model.

This is a study that will run for 5 years, with 2 seasons Before and 3 seasons After dam construction, and will sample 50 sites (25 above and 25 below dams) at 5 facilities (5 sites above and below at each dam). We planning for 3 repeat visits per year at each site, which will consist of Time Constrained Searches to record larval abundance. We consider the sites 'closed' within a year (although there could be changes due to emigration/immigration), but 'open' among years.

Given this dynamics, we decided that the data gathered will be used in pcountOpen for detecting potential population changes by testing for the Before/After Control/Impact interaction in the recruitment and apparent survival terms (similar to a study we performed using dynamic occupancy models, where we tested for the BACI interaction in the extinction and colonization terms; Popescu et al (2012) Ecol Apps 22:1389-1404). I simulating abundance data with high yearly survival and complementary recruitment rate (for population stationarity) and an impact on apparent survival (from season to season, not within season) during the After period at the Impact (below dam) sites.

The simulated datasets look good, but the models do not seem to be able to detect even drastic decreases in apparent survival (80%). I wonder if the problem is with the way I am setting the Before/After and Control/Impact variables (see below). I set them in a similar manner with colext, where 5 years require 4 transitions (1 column for Before, since there are 2 Before years, and 3 columns for After; with transition between Yr2 and Yr3 being the first After period). The last column is being ignored. Or should I do B for the first 2 years and A for the last 3?

SiteType   Yr1   Yr2  Yr3  Yr4  Yr5
-------------------------------------------------------
Impct        B      A     A    A     None                    # this is for 25 Impact sites
Ctrl           B      A     A    A     None                    # this is for 25 Control sites

I am using the Before/After setup as yearlySiteCovs, and SiteType as siteCovs.

The pcountOpen model (see below) fails to correctly estimate the simulated decrease in survival, and this points to 2 potential issues: (1) either the BACI variables are not setup correctly, or (2) apparent survival is estimated WITHIN, not between years (in which case the pcountOpen model might not be appropriate for our problem). Is there a way to differentiate between within- and among-year survival? Any thoughts on this would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you

Cheers,
Viorel

#### Simulation and Analysis R code ######################################

# s=apparent survival Before (Control and Impact sites) and After (Control sites only)
# sA=apparent survival After at Impact sites only
# p=detection probability
# siteT=number of Impact sites
# yearB=number of years Before
# yearA=number of years After
# nyear=total number of years (primary periods)
# n_vis=number of visits per year (secondary periods)

dataset <- function(sA, s=0.9, nyear=5, n_sites=50, n_vis=3, p=0.8, siteT=25,
                    yearB=2, yearA=nyear-yearB) {

  tab <- matrix(rep(0, nyear*n_sites), ncol=nyear)        # matrix for storing true abundance values
  tab <- as.data.frame(tab)
  names(tab) <- paste("t", 1:nyear, sep="")

  obsab <- matrix(rep(0, nyear*n_sites*n_vis), ncol=(nyear*n_vis),
                   dimnames=list(paste("site", 1:n_sites, sep=""), paste("Yr", rep(1:nyear, each=n_vis), "v", 1:n_vis, sep="")))
  obsab <- as.data.frame(obsab)                                # matrix for storing observed abundance values

# simulate true and observed abundances

  for (i in 1:n_sites) {

    tab[i,1] = rnbinom(1, size=2.31, mu=6.70)                    # Simulate true abundance at t1 using a negative binomial distribution

    obsab[i,1:n_vis] = rbinom(n_vis, tab[i,1], p)                   # Simulate observed abundance at t1 using detection prob. p

    for(t in 2:nyear) {
      tab[i,t] <- rbinom(1,tab[i,t-1],s) + round(tab[i,t-1]*(1-s))  # abundance in subsequent years depends on apparent survival and recruitment
                                                                                     # we assume population stationarity

          for(j in 1:n_vis) {
            obsab[i,((t-1)*n_vis)+j] = rbinom(1, tab[i, t], p)         # observed data incorporates detection probability
          }
    }
  }

  ### Then simulate the Treatment sites After Impact portion of the tab and obsab matrices
  ### use the After (assumed) parameter values at Treatment Impacted sites only.
  ### The structure is similar to the previous Site 'for' loop

  for(i in 1:siteT) {                 # use the Treatment sites only

    for(tt in (yearB+1):nyear) {
      tab[i,tt] <- rbinom(1,tab[i,tt-1],sA) + round(tab[i,tt-1]*(1-s))          # abundance in subsequent years depends on apparent survival and recruitment

      for(j in 1:n_vis) {
        obsab[i,((tt-1)*n_vis)+j] = rbinom(1, tab[i, tt], p)   # observed data incorporates detection probability
      }
    }
  }

  ### Add a column to observed data for site type (Control or Treatment)
  obsab$treat = factor(c(rep('TRT', siteT), rep('CTRL', n_sites-siteT)))

  ### Create a matrix of yearly site covariates containing factors Before and After
  years.Before = matrix(rep("Before", n_sites*(yearB-1)), ncol=(yearB-1))
  years.After = matrix(rep("After", n_sites*yearA), ncol=yearA)
  years.None = matrix(rep("None", n_sites*1), ncol=1)
  years.BA = cbind(years.Before, years.After, years.None)
  years.BA = as.data.frame(years.BA)
  colnames(years.BA) <- paste("Yr", rep(1:nyear), sep="")

  ### Combine the observed P/A data and the yearly covariates (Years)
  obsab1=cbind(obsab, years.BA)

  return(data.frame(cbind(obsab1)))
}

require(unmarked)

analysis = function(Cdata, s=0.9, nyear=5, n_sites=50, n_vis=3, p=0.8, siteT=25,
                    yearB=2, yearA=nyear-yearB) {

  #####################################################################
  ### Prepare data for 'unmarked', Dail-Madsen model

  # prepare the matrix for observed data
  yMat = Cdata[,1:(nyear*n_vis)]

  # prepare the matrix for Before/After : B and A periods had to be introduced as yearlySiteCovs
  BAMat = Cdata[,((nyear*n_vis)+2):((nyear*n_vis)+1+nyear)]
  yearlies = data.frame(BA = matrix(t(BAMat)))

  # prepare the multi-year pcountOpen data.frame
  umf <- unmarkedFramePCO(
    y=yMat,
    siteCovs=Cdata[,"treat", drop=F],
    yearlySiteCovs=yearlies,
    numPrimary=nyear)

  ### Run 2 models
  Null.fit <- pcountOpen(~1, ~1, ~treat+BA, ~1, umf, mixture="NB", K=50)
  Alt.fit <- pcountOpen(~1, ~1, ~treat*BA, ~1, umf, mixture="NB", K=50)

  list(Null.fit = Null.fit, Alt.fit = Alt.fit)
}

Hi Viorel,

For a study with 5 primary periods, there are 4 transitions, so you should have: B, B, A, A, NA; not B, A, A, A, NA. Also, I don't think that you are simulating data according to the default model (dynamics="constant"). For that model, the number of survivors is binomial, and the number of recruits is Poisson. There is an example on the help page. Hope this helps.

Richard

messages.body_plain:
Hello, folks.

I have been trying to replicate the gmultmix N-mixture models in JAGS, for a removal design with both primary and secondary periods. I may have succeeded in the optimal case where there are no missing data (thanks to Richard Chandler for the idea of the sequential binomial trials for the removal part), but things rapidly fall apart once I introduce a missing data point or two (either for the catch data or covariates). Does anyone have any idea of how to get the code fully generalizable to allow missing data? And any suggestions to optimize the code for speed? It is darn slow... which is not surprising, I'm fairly new to WinBUGS and brand-new with JAGS.

Thanks in advance for any advice or pointers.
cheers, Jessi Brown

Code appended below:

# my attempt at making JAGS code for
# the Chandler et al. 2011 temporary
# emigration N-mixture models
# removal design with secondary samples

library(unmarked)
library(rjags)
load.module("glm")

# generating some data

# Data dimensions
nSites <- 200
nSecondary <- 3
nPrimary <- 6

# Parameters
expit <- function(x) {
    1/(1+exp(-x))
}

# dummy variable to assign sites to one of two areas
area <- round(runif(nSites, 0, 1))

# super-population calculation
lambda0 <- log(200)  #5.298317
lambda1 <- log(100)-log(200) # area1 sites are less well-populated, -0.6931472
lambda <- exp(lambda0 + lambda1*area)        # mean abundance in primary period 1

# linear availability for capture; max at -2 temp
temp <- array(NA, c(nSites, nPrimary))
for(t in 1:nPrimary){
    temp[,t] <- runif(nSites, -2, 2)
}
phi0 <- -1.5459
phi1 <- -1.1422
phi <- expit(phi0 + phi1*temp)       # availability for capture

# unimodal detection probability; max at 0 time, each secondary sample
# follows in sequence
time <- array(NA, c(nSites, nSecondary, nPrimary))
for(t in 1:nPrimary){
    time[,1,t] <- runif(nSites, -2, 2)
    time[,2,t] <- time[,1,t] + abs(rnorm(nSites, 0.1, 0.05))
    time[,3,t] <- time[,2,t] + abs(rnorm(nSites, 0.1, 0.05))
    }
time2 <- time*time
p0 <- -2.1969
p1 <- 0
p2 <- -0.95069
p <- expit(p0 + p1*time + p2*time*time)    # detection probability

# Super-population size
set.seed(458)
M <- rpois(nSites, lambda)

# Population size during each primary sampling period
N <- matrix(NA, nSites, nPrimary)

# Observed counts
y <- array(NA, c(nSites, nSecondary, nPrimary))

for(i in 1:nSites) {
    for(j in 1:nPrimary) {
        N[i,] <- rbinom(nPrimary, M[i], phi[i,j])
        for(k in 1:nSecondary) {
            y[i,1,] <- rbinom(nPrimary, N[i,j], p[i,k,j])
            Nleft1 <- N[i,j] - y[i,1,j]
            y[i,2,] <- rbinom(nPrimary, Nleft1, p[i,k,j])
            Nleft2 <- Nleft1 - y[i,2,j]
            y[i,3,] <- rbinom(nPrimary, Nleft2, p[i,k,j])
            }
        }
}

plot(1:nPrimary, colSums(N), xlab="Primary period", ylab="Population available", type="o")

#############################################################
#
#  on to JAGS model
#  attempted removal model
#
#############################################################

sink(file="temp_em_covs.txt")
cat("
model {
lambda.int <http://lambda.int> ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
lambda.beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
phi.int <http://phi.int> ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
phi.beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
p.int <http://p.int> ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
p.beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
p.beta2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)

for(i in 1:nSites) {
  M[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
  log(lambda[i]) <- lambda.int <http://lambda.int> + lambda.beta1*area[i]
  for(j in 1:nPrimary) {
      N[i,j] ~ dbin(phi[i,j], M[i])
      logit(phi[i,j]) <- phi.int <http://phi.int> + phi.beta1*temp[i,j]
      for(k in 1:nSecondary) {
          logit(p[i,k,j]) <- p.int <http://p.int> + p.beta1*time[i,k,j] + p.beta2*time2[i,k,j]
     }
      y[i,1,j] ~ dbin(p[i,1,j], N[i,j])
      y[i,2,j] ~ dbin(p[i,2,j], N[i,j]-y[i,1,j])
      y[i,3,j] ~ dbin(p[i,3,j], N[i,j]-y[i,1,j]-y[i,2,j])
      }
  }
}

", fill=TRUE)
sink()

# Format data and create function to initiate parameters
Mst <- apply(y, 1, function(x) {
             if(all(is.na <http://is.na>(x)))
                 return(2)
             else
                 return(sum(x, na.rm = TRUE) + 30)
         })

dat.cov <- list(nSites=nSites, nPrimary=nPrimary, nSecondary=nSecondary, y=y, area=area, temp=temp, time=time, time2=time2)
init.cov <- function() list(lambda.int <http://lambda.int>=rnorm(1), lambda.beta1=rnorm(1), phi.int <http://phi.int>=rnorm(1), phi.beta1=rnorm(1), p.int <http://p.int>=rnorm(1), p.beta1=rnorm(1), p.beta2=rnorm(1), M=Mst)
pars.cov <- c("lambda.int <http://lambda.int>", "lambda.beta1", "phi.int <http://phi.int>", "phi.beta1", "p.int <http://p.int>", "p.beta1", "p.beta2")

# Compile the model.
jm.cov <- jags.model("temp_em_covs.txt", dat.cov, init.cov, n.chains=2, n.adapt=5000)
# seems very sensitive to the initial values for Mst

# Draw samples from the posterior
jc.cov <- coda.samples(jm.cov, pars.cov, n.iter=10000)
# View the Markov chains
plot(jc.cov, ask=T)
summary(jc.cov) # coefficients generally in ballpark especially when run longer
# MCMC diagnostics
gelman.diag(jc.cov)    # Should be ~ <1.1
autocorr.plot(jc.cov)  # If samples are autocorrelated, you need more iters
crosscorr(jc.cov)      # Correlation among parameters

# try putting an NA in or two; uncomment to choose which data gets NA
# "fix" by just putting a zero back in
# time[1,1,5] <- NA
y[1,1:3,5] <- NA
# temp[1,5] <- 0

             if(all(is.na <http://is.na>(x)))
                 return(2)
             else
                 return(sum(x, na.rm = TRUE) + 30)
         })

dat.cov <- list(nSites=nSites, nPrimary=nPrimary, nSecondary=nSecondary, y=y, area=area, temp=temp, time=time, time2=time2)
init.cov <- function() list(lambda.int <http://lambda.int>=rnorm(1), lambda.beta1=rnorm(1), phi.int <http://phi.int>=rnorm(1), phi.beta1=rnorm(1), p.int <http://p.int>=rnorm(1), p.beta1=rnorm(1), p.beta2=rnorm(1), M=Mst)

# Compile the model.

Hi Jessi,

I would definitely recommend Marc Kéry's "Bayesian Population Analysis with WinBUGS" book (with Michael Schaub) if you are serious about running these models in JAGS.  The book provides WinBUGS code but they include an R script with everything converted to JAGS as well (changes are minor).  They'll have tips on optimizing these models and where you can sometimes gain efficiencies.

As for the missing data, there should be no problem with having NAs in the response variable.  Covariates definitely need values though and one solution is to standardize the covariate values for which measurements exist and then set all the NAs to 0 (effectively assigning missing values the mean).  There are some implications of doing this that are beyond the scope of my comment - I believe some discussion can be found in the Program MARK book.  But so long as the proportion of NAs in the covariate are relatively small it shouldn't be a problem.

hi all,
 I agree with Shannon on this, you should generally avoid setting the missing covariates to the mean value. (in the case of a categorical variable, this would probably be the modal value).
 If there are very few missing values then this is probably not a terrible thing to do, but otherwise I suggest putting a prior distribution on the covariate and, in this case, BUGS/JAGS will do imputation automatically by filling in the missing values with draws from the posterior distribution.   For a categorical random variable you could do this simply by putting:  x[i] ~ dcat(probs)
or similar, and then specifying a prior distribution for the elements of "probs".
For example, if the variable has 3 levels then you might do:

for(i in 1:3){
alpha[i] ~ dgamma(1,1)
probs[i]<- alpha[i]/sum(alpha[])
}

which I think imposes a Dirichlet prior distribution on "probs".
In this way, the analysis will properly account for uncertainty about the missing covariate values.

For likelihood methods this is less easy to do. As Shannon said, see the standard methods for EM and similar methods.

regards
andy

one follow-up:
 having the offset in there changes the response to "individuals per unit area" (i.e., density) and you probably need the offset if sample areas are very different because in most cases that is an important source of variation.
 Having the offset in the model implies that population size scales linearly with area. i.e., E[N] = Area*lambda
 If you estimate the effect of area, then you are allowing for a slower or faster rate off increase in population size as Area changes. I think there are probably a lot of biological mechanisms that might lead to one or the other (faster or slower increases) and so it seems sensible to estimate the effect in general.

regards
andy

messages.body_plain:
The person that expressed this concern to Erynn provided her with some example R code to illustrate the situation.  But this example code only illustrated what happens when you improperly include an offset.  They simulated random counts that were completely unrelated to area (i.e., no scaling relationship) and the resulting Poisson regression with area as both an offset and a covariate estimated a significant coefficient for area.  That's because the offset should not have been included in the first place!  The code below shows this problem.

When count is unrelated to area, the regression with area as both an
offset and a covariate estimates a significant coefficient = -1, which
is obviously counteracting the improperly imposed +1 coefficient for the
 offset.  Anyway, this may be elementary for some but I thought it
further supported the logic that Andy provided.

#----------------------------------------------------------#
n=100
area=rlnorm(n,3,2)
lambda <- 3
coeff <- 0.5  # coefficient for the covariate effect

# generate random counts that do NOT depend on area
count=rpois(n,lambda)
# generate random counts that DO depend on area (remove hash to use)
#count<-sapply(area,function(x){rpois(1,exp(log(lambda) + log(x) + coeff*(log(x))))})

models <- list()
# Both offset and covariate
models[[1]] <- glm(count~offset(log(area))+I(log(area)),family="poisson")
# Only covariate
models[[2]] <- glm(count~I(log(area)),family="poisson")
# Only offset
models[[3]] <- glm(count~offset(log(area)),family="poisson")
# Neither (intercept only)
models[[4]] <- glm(count~1,family="poisson")

lapply(models,summary)
#----------------------------------------------------------#
